title: Stanley Druckenmiller makes AI writing a billionaire flex
source: Axios — Stanley Druckenmiller makes AI writing a billionaire flex (2026-08-26)
body: Legendary investor Stanley Druckenmiller made AI writing seem like no big deal this week, telling NOTUS reporter Jeff Stein "of course" he used it to help draft a widely shared op-ed for the Wall Street Journal . Why it matters: The moment could mark a real cultural shift where AI writing is basically all good, at least among a certain set of influential elites. Where it stands: Among his intended audience in the financial world, Druckenmiller's article got more attention for its substance — a scathing critique of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent — than for its style. The writing is infused with the telltale cadences of the AI-generated one-two punch — for example, "If the 30-year must trade at 5.5% to clear, that isn't a crisis. It is an invoice." Or this familiar construct: "This wasn't liquidity management, it was price management ... " State of play: Many folks on "fintwits," the finance community on X, formerly known as Twitter, not only seemed willing to overlook the method, but praised it: "Druck using AI to write the op ed is the sickest burn of 2026," Claudia Sahm, a former economist for the Federal Reserve posted . "Didn't even waste his time writing up why Bessent was wrong." The big picture: The WSJ's opinions section threw open the floodgates to more AI-generated op-eds in its response to the discourse. "AI is a fact of modern life. People will use it to assist in their work and writing, including with research, checking grammar, editing and more," WSJ opinion editor Paul Gigot said in a statement. "The question for us is whether what we publish from contributors reflects an author's original argument, and if the author has the standing and credibility to make it." "In Stan Druckenmiller's case, we have had a relationship with him for many years, and nobody can doubt that his op-ed is his genuine opinion." Worth noting: The WSJ newsroom, separate from Gigot's team, has a different policy on AI use. Friction point: The reaction was very different to the response earlier this month when Harvard professor Ricardo Hausmann was criticized for using AI to write a column for the Financial Times . The paper ultimately appended a note at the top: "It has come to our attention that AI was used to condense a longer draft of this column prior to submission to the FT and our own editorial involvement." "The FT editorial code of conduct specifically prohibits the use of AI in the writing process." Zoom in: Druckenmiller likened using AI to using a calculator. "There's a reason I moved from an English major to being an economics major," Druckenmiller told Stein. "I'm not embarrassed by it ... I write everything using AI now for the same reason I use a calculator when I do math problems." Between the lines: For the most part, plenty of billionaires already employ ghostwriters to spin up their op-eds, LinkedIn musings and social media posts. Transitioning to AI seems like a natural progression. Zoom out: For everyone else, it's not clear yet if they can get away with this. Druckenmiller's AI-gate comes in the context of a broader backlash to the intersection of AI and content. YouTuber Hank Green faced backlash after viewers of a video last month accused him of using AI to write his script. He later shared an policy on how he'll use the tech going forward. "Where do you draw the line of what's immoral and what is moral?" content creator and marketing strategist Sam Ogborn told Axios. Madison Mills contributed reporting.
